title: India Just Fell to Seventh in the Global Stock Market Rankings. AI Took Its Place.
excerpt: Taiwan and South Korea overtook India in rapid succession as the global AI investment boom bypassed the world's fastest-growing major economy. Foreign investors have pulled $26.4 billion from Indian equities in 2026.
body:
It happened in the span of a few weeks, and it happened quietly. First Taiwan overtook India in total stock market capitalisation. Then South Korea followed. By early June, what was once emerging Asia's darling had slipped to seventh in the world — behind the United States, China, Japan, the United Kingdom, Taiwan, and South Korea.

The numbers, compiled by Reuters, tell a story that goes beyond a ranking shuffle. India's share in the MSCI Global Standard Index has contracted to 12.3 per cent from a peak of 21 per cent in September 2024. Foreign portfolio investors have pulled $26.4 billion from Indian equities so far in 2026, putting the country on course to far surpass the record $18.9 billion outflow of 2025. And the engine driving capital away from India and into East Asia has a single name: artificial intelligence.

## The AI Gap

Taiwan's stock market has tripled since 2020, driven almost entirely by the AI-fuelled surge in semiconductor stocks. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company alone accounts for more than 40 per cent of Taiwan's total market capitalisation. TSMC posted net income of roughly $18 billion for Q1 2026, up 58 per cent year-on-year, with high-performance computing — the backbone of AI workloads — making up 61 per cent of first-quarter sales.

South Korea tells a similar story. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, both critical to the global AI supply chain through their memory and chip businesses, powered a rally that earned both countries Goldman Sachs ratings upgrades last week.

India has no equivalent. No single company in the Nifty 50 or BSE Sensex plays the role that TSMC plays in Taipei or Samsung plays in Seoul. India's IT services giants — Infosys, TCS, Wipro — are downstream users and integrators of AI technology, not the hardware providers that capture the bulk of the investment flow.

"Without the equivalent of a TSMC or an SK Hynix, it's hard to imagine that capital making its way back to India anytime soon," Reuters noted in its India File analysis.

## Not All Lost

Some analysts push back on the doom narrative. Abhay Laijawala, managing director and India chief investment officer at Lighthouse Canton, argues that India offers a "picks-and-shovels" opportunity in the AI era — investments tied to electricity generation, cooling systems, physical infrastructure, and data centres that underpin the broader AI ecosystem. India's index is also more diversified than Taiwan's or South Korea's, where a single sector dominates.

And there was a silver lining this week. After South Korea's chip stocks suffered a sharp correction — Samsung and SK Hynix both tumbled, pushing Korea's market cap down 10 per cent from its peak — India briefly reclaimed sixth place, with its total market capitalisation at $4.84 trillion versus South Korea's $4.5 trillion.

But the broader trend remains clear. India's 7.7 per cent decline in the Nifty and 9.1 per cent fall in the Sensex since the start of the Iran war have compounded the problem. Record foreign outflows, elevated crude oil prices squeezing corporate margins, and the weakening rupee have made India less attractive to the global capital that once poured in with conviction.

## What NRI Investors Should Watch

For the millions of non-resident Indians with exposure to Indian equities — whether through direct stock holdings, mutual funds, or NPS accounts — the ranking slip is more than a headline. It reflects a structural challenge: India's weight in global indices is shrinking, which means passive funds that track those indices are automatically reducing their India allocation.

The RBI's recent move to double NRI investment limits in listed Indian companies from 5 per cent to 10 per cent (and raise the aggregate ceiling from 10 to 24 per cent) may help attract some diaspora capital. But bridging the gap will require something India's market currently lacks — a globally dominant AI hardware champion.

The Sensex gained 0.54 per cent on Tuesday, led by banking stocks rallying on the RBI's new forex swap facility. But markets are braced for another volatile session on Wednesday as renewed US strikes on Iran cloud the outlook for energy prices and global risk appetite.

India's economy is still the fastest-growing among the world's largest. Its stock market, for now, is telling a different story.
